read.title: Why does it rain so much in the UK?
read.intro: Read this carefully — the questions afterwards will ask you to use the ideas, not just remember them.
body: Ask anyone abroad what they know about British weather and they will probably say one word: rain. It is a bit unfair — Rome gets more rain in a year than London does — but parts of the UK really are among the wettest places in Europe. To understand why, you need to know where our air comes from and what happens to it when it arrives.
## Where our weather comes from

The UK sits on the western edge of Europe with the Atlantic Ocean on one side. Most of the time, the wind blows towards us from the south-west. These are called the **prevailing winds**, and because they have travelled thousands of kilometres across warm ocean water, they pick up huge amounts of moisture through evaporation. By the time this air reaches us it is mild and damp.

The ocean also keeps our temperatures steady. A warm ocean current called the **North Atlantic Drift** carries heat from the Caribbean towards our coast. That is why the UK has mild winters compared with places at the same latitude, such as parts of Canada, which freeze solid. Geographers call our type of climate a **temperate maritime** climate: not too hot, not too cold, and wet all year round.
## The key idea: rising air makes rain

Every kind of rain starts the same way. When air rises, it expands and cools. Cool air cannot hold as much water vapour as warm air, so once the air cools to a certain temperature — its **dew point** — the water vapour **condenses** into tiny droplets. Billions of these droplets make a cloud. When the droplets join together and become heavy enough, they fall as rain.
So the real question is: what makes air rise? There are three main answers, and they give us the three types of rainfall.
## 1. Relief rainfall

When moist air blowing in from the Atlantic hits high ground — such as the mountains of Wales, the Lake District or the Scottish Highlands — it is forced upwards. As it rises it cools, condenses and drops its rain on the side of the mountain facing the wind (the **windward** side). By the time the air sinks down the other side, most of its moisture has gone. The sinking air warms up, so clouds evaporate and the land beyond is much drier. This dry area is called a **rain shadow**.

This is the main reason the west of the UK is so much wetter than the east. Seathwaite in the Lake District can receive over 3,000 mm of rain a year, while parts of East Anglia get only around 600 mm — five times less.
## 2. Frontal rainfall

Large masses of air with different temperatures often meet over the Atlantic. Where warm air meets cold air, the boundary is called a **front**. Warm air is lighter, so it is pushed up over the cold air. As it rises, it cools and condenses, giving long periods of steady rain. Fronts usually come with **depressions** — areas of low pressure that sweep in from the west, bringing wind, cloud and rain. A typical British autumn might bring a new depression every few days.
## 3. Convectional rainfall

On a hot summer day, the sun heats the ground, which heats the air above it. This warm air rises quickly in currents, cools, and forms tall, towering clouds. The result can be a sudden heavy downpour, sometimes with thunder and lightning, usually in the afternoon. This type is common in the tropics every day, but in the UK it mainly happens in summer, especially in the south-east, where it is warmest.
## Putting it together

The UK gets so much rain because moist Atlantic air arrives almost constantly, and something nearly always lifts it: mountains in the west, fronts from passing depressions, or summer heating. Understanding *why* air rises is the key to explaining almost any rainfall pattern on a map — which is exactly what exam questions love to ask.

keywords.def: The direction the wind blows from most often. In the UK it is from the south-west.
When water vapour (a gas) cools and turns into liquid water droplets.
The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapour starts to condense.
A dry area on the side of a mountain sheltered from the wind.
The boundary where a warm air mass meets a cold air mass.
An area of low air pressure, usually bringing wind, cloud and rain.

questions.q: From which direction does the UK's prevailing wind usually blow?
options: North-east
South-west
South-east
North-west
questions.explain: The prevailing winds come from the south-west, across the Atlantic Ocean, which is why they bring so much moisture.

questions.q: Why is air arriving from the Atlantic so moist?
options: It has passed over mountains
It comes from the Arctic
It has picked up water vapour by evaporation over the ocean
It has been heated by the sun over land
questions.explain: Travelling thousands of kilometres over the sea, the air gains moisture through evaporation from the ocean surface.

questions.q: What happens to air as it rises?
options: It expands and cools
It shrinks and warms
It gets heavier
It gains more water vapour
questions.explain: Rising air expands and cools. Cooler air holds less water vapour, which is why rising air leads to cloud and rain.

questions.q: What is the dew point?
options: The height at which clouds form rain
The temperature at which water vapour starts to condense
The point where two air masses meet
The wettest place on a mountain
questions.explain: The dew point is a temperature. When air cools to it, water vapour condenses into droplets.

questions.q: Which type of rainfall is mainly responsible for the west of the UK being wetter than the east?
options: Convectional
Frontal
Acid rain
Relief
questions.explain: Relief rainfall: moist south-westerly air is forced up over the western mountains and drops most of its rain there.

questions.q: A town lies on the eastern side of a mountain range, with the prevailing wind from the west. What would you expect its rainfall to be like?
options: Drier, because it is in a rain shadow
Wetter, because it is on the windward side
The same as the west side
Wetter, because sinking air causes rain
questions.explain: With a westerly wind, the east side is sheltered (leeward). The air has already lost its moisture and is sinking and warming, so it is a rain shadow.

questions.q: In frontal rainfall, why is the warm air pushed upwards?
options: Because it is heavier than cold air
Because the sun heats it
Because it is lighter than cold air
Because it hits a mountain
questions.explain: Warm air is less dense (lighter) than cold air, so it rises over the cold air at a front, then cools and condenses.

questions.q: A sudden heavy thunderstorm on a hot July afternoon in Kent is most likely to be:
options: Relief rainfall
Convectional rainfall
Frontal rainfall
Caused by the North Atlantic Drift
questions.explain: Strong heating of the ground makes warm air rise rapidly, forming tall clouds and heavy, short-lived storms — convectional rainfall, most common in the warm south-east in summer.

questions.q: Why does the UK have milder winters than parts of Canada at the same latitude?
options: The UK is closer to the equator
The UK has more mountains
Depressions bring warm air every day
The North Atlantic Drift brings warm water towards the UK
questions.explain: The North Atlantic Drift carries warmth from the Caribbean, keeping UK winters mild for our latitude.

questions.q: Seathwaite gets about 3,000 mm of rain a year and parts of East Anglia about 600 mm. How many times wetter is Seathwaite?
options: About 5 times
About 2 times
About 50 times
About 10 times
questions.explain: 3,000 ÷ 600 = 5. Being able to compare figures like this is a common skill in geography exams.

sessions.reflect: In two or three sentences, explain to someone in your class why Wales is wetter than Norfolk. Try to use the words 'relief', 'condense' and 'rain shadow'.

read.title: The periodic table: a map of everything
read.intro: Elements, atoms, symbols — and the Russian chemist who predicted elements nobody had found yet.
body: Everything around you — the air, your phone, the bus seat, your own body — is made from a surprisingly small set of ingredients called **elements**. Scientists know of 118 of them. About 90 occur naturally on Earth; the rest have only ever been made in laboratories, sometimes lasting for less than a second. The **periodic table** is how chemists organise all of them on a single page, and once you know how to read it, it tells you an enormous amount.
## What is an element?

An element is a substance made of only one type of **atom**. Gold is an element: a gold ring is made of trillions upon trillions of gold atoms and nothing else. Oxygen is an element too. Water, however, is not. Water is a **compound**: it is made of hydrogen atoms and oxygen atoms chemically joined together. An element cannot be broken down into anything simpler by a chemical reaction, which is exactly why elements are the building blocks for everything else.
## Inside an atom

Atoms are almost unimaginably small. Lined up side by side, tens of millions of them would fit across your fingernail. Yet each one has a structure. In the centre is a tiny **nucleus** containing **protons**, which have a positive charge, and **neutrons**, which have no charge. Around the nucleus move even tinier **electrons**, which have a negative charge.

The number of protons is what makes each element different from every other. Every hydrogen atom has 1 proton. Every carbon atom has 6. Every gold atom has 79. If an atom had 78 protons instead, it would not be gold at all — it would be platinum. This number is called the **atomic number**, and it is the order the modern periodic table follows: hydrogen is element 1, helium is 2, lithium is 3, and so on, all the way to oganesson, element 118.
## Symbols: chemistry's shorthand

Each element has a **chemical symbol** of one or two letters. The first letter is always a capital, and the second letter, if there is one, is always lower case. Many symbols are easy to guess: O for oxygen, C for carbon, Ca for calcium, Cl for chlorine.

Others look strange because they come from old Latin names. Sodium is Na, from *natrium*. Iron is Fe, from *ferrum*. Gold is Au, from *aurum*. Lead is Pb, from *plumbum* — which is also where the word 'plumber' comes from, because Roman water pipes were made of lead.

The capital-letter rule really matters. Co is cobalt, a single metallic element. CO, with two capitals, means one carbon atom joined to one oxygen atom: carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas. One small letter changes everything.
## Mendeleev's brilliant gamble

By the 1860s, chemists had discovered about 63 elements, but nobody had found a convincing way to organise them. A Russian chemistry professor called **Dmitri Mendeleev** wrote each element and its properties on a separate card and moved the cards around, a bit like laying out a game of patience. In 1869 he published his table. He put the elements in order of the mass of their atoms, and placed elements with similar properties in the same column.

Mendeleev's stroke of genius was what he *didn't* do. Where an element did not fit the pattern, he refused to force it in. Instead he left **gaps**, insisting that they belonged to elements that had not been discovered yet. He even predicted what those missing elements would be like.

Below aluminium, for example, he predicted a metal he called 'eka-aluminium', and described its density and its low melting point. In 1875 a French chemist discovered a new element, gallium — and its properties matched Mendeleev's predictions remarkably closely. Gallium melts at about 30 °C, so a lump of it will melt in your hand. When germanium was discovered in 1886, it fitted neatly into another of his gaps. Other scientists were won over: the table was not just a tidy list, but a pattern that revealed something real about nature.

Mendeleev also swapped a few elements round when ordering them by mass put them in the wrong column. He placed tellurium before iodine, even though tellurium atoms are heavier, because iodine clearly belonged with chlorine and bromine. In 1913 a young British physicist, Henry Moseley, showed that the true order is by atomic number, not by mass. Tellurium has 52 protons and iodine has 53 — so in the modern table they sit exactly where Mendeleev had put them.
## Why it matters

The modern periodic table is arranged so that elements with similar properties line up in columns. That means if you know about one element, you can make good predictions about its neighbours, just as Mendeleev did. In the next science session you will learn to read the table like a map — and find out why a soft metal that fizzes in water and a gas that never reacts at all can sit on the same chart.

keywords.def: A substance made of only one type of atom. It cannot be broken down into anything simpler by chemical reactions.
The smallest particle of an element. It has a nucleus (protons and neutrons) with electrons around it.
A substance made of two or more different elements chemically joined, e.g. water (H₂O).
The number of protons in an atom. The modern periodic table is in order of atomic number.
One or two letters standing for an element. First letter capital, second letter lower case, e.g. Na.
Russian chemist who published the first successful periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for undiscovered elements.

questions.q: What is an element?
options: A mixture of different types of atom
A substance made of only one type of atom
Two or more different elements chemically joined
Any substance that is a solid at room temperature
questions.explain: An element contains only one type of atom — for example, gold contains only gold atoms. Option C describes a compound, and elements can be solids, liquids or gases.

questions.q: Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen atoms chemically joined together. What is water?
options: A compound
An element
A mixture of two elements
A single atom
questions.explain: When atoms of different elements are chemically joined, they form a compound. A mixture is different: its parts are not chemically joined and can often be separated easily, like sand and salt.

questions.q: What does the atomic number of an element tell you?
options: The number of neutrons in its atoms
The mass of one of its atoms
The year it was discovered
The number of protons in its atoms
questions.explain: The atomic number is the number of protons. It is what makes each element unique — every carbon atom has 6 protons, every gold atom 79.

questions.q: Which is the correct chemical symbol for sodium?
options: So
S
Na
SO
questions.explain: Sodium is Na, from its Latin name natrium. S is sulfur, and SO would mean sulfur and oxygen together.

questions.q: A student writes the symbol for cobalt as 'CO'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — it is correct
The second letter should be lower case; CO means carbon and oxygen
Cobalt's symbol is Cb
Symbols can only ever have one letter
questions.explain: Cobalt is Co. A second capital letter means a second element: CO is carbon monoxide, a compound of carbon and oxygen. The capital-letter rule matters!

questions.q: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his table?
options: He ran out of space on his cards
The gaps were for compounds
To separate metals from non-metals
He believed some elements had not been discovered yet
questions.explain: Mendeleev trusted his pattern. Where no known element fitted, he left a gap for an element still to be found — and predicted its properties.

questions.q: What convinced other scientists that Mendeleev's table was right?
options: Elements discovered later matched his predictions
He was the most famous chemist in Europe
He had discovered most of the elements himself
It was in alphabetical order, so it was easy to use
questions.explain: Gallium (1875) and germanium (1886) fitted his gaps and had the properties he had predicted. A good scientific idea makes predictions that turn out to be true.

questions.q: An element has 17 protons in each atom. Where would it appear in the modern periodic table?
options: Next to the element with 34 protons
At the very start of the table
Between the elements with 16 and 18 protons
It depends on how heavy its atoms are
questions.explain: The modern table is in order of atomic number (protons), so element 17 (chlorine) sits between element 16 (sulfur) and element 18 (argon). Mass doesn't decide the order.

questions.q: Mendeleev published his table in 1869, and gallium was discovered in 1875. How many years did his prediction take to be confirmed?
options: 6 years
4 years
16 years
60 years
questions.explain: 1875 − 1869 = 6 years. Only six years after he published, an element turned up with almost exactly the properties he had predicted.

questions.q: Tellurium atoms are heavier than iodine atoms, yet tellurium comes first in the modern table. Why?
options: Mendeleev made a mistake that was never corrected
Tellurium was discovered first
The table is ordered by atomic number, and tellurium has fewer protons
Iodine is a gas, so it goes later
questions.explain: Tellurium has 52 protons and iodine 53. Moseley showed in 1913 that atomic number, not mass, is the true order — proving Mendeleev's swap was right. (Iodine is actually a solid.)

sessions.reflect: Imagine explaining to a Year 6 pupil why Mendeleev leaving gaps in his table was such a clever idea. Write two or three sentences.

read.title: Rich world, poor world: measuring development
read.intro: How do geographers decide how 'developed' a country is — and why is one number never enough?
body: Imagine two babies born on the same day: one in Manchester, the other in Niamey, the capital of Niger in West Africa. Before either of them has done anything at all, the place they were born has already shaped their chances in life. The baby in Manchester can expect to live to around 81. The baby in Niger can expect to live to a little over 60 — roughly twenty years less. The baby in Niger is also far less likely to finish school, see a doctor regularly or have clean water piped into their home. Geographers use the word **development** to describe differences like these.
## What is development?

Development means the progress a country makes in improving the lives of its people. It is not just about money. It also includes health, education, safe housing, clean water and the freedom to make choices about your own life.

Geographers often separate two ideas. **Standard of living** is about wealth and the material things people have — a home, enough food, a fridge, a phone. **Quality of life** is broader: it is about how well people live, which also includes health, safety, friendships and happiness. A person can have a high standard of living but a poor quality of life, for example if they are rich but live somewhere unsafe.
## Measuring development
You cannot measure 'quality of life' with a ruler, so geographers use **development indicators**: statistics that can be compared between countries. Some of the most common are:

**GDP per capita** — the total value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by its population. It gives a rough idea of how much wealth there is per person. In 2023 it was around $49,000 in the UK, but only around $600 in Niger. ('Per capita' is Latin for 'per head'.) Because it is about money, this is an **economic indicator**.
**Life expectancy** — the average number of years a person can expect to live.
**Infant mortality rate** — the number of babies, out of every 1,000 born alive, who die before their first birthday. In the UK it is about 4. In some of the world's poorest countries it is over 50.
**Literacy rate** — the percentage of adults who can read and write.
**Access to clean water** — the percentage of people who can get safe drinking water.
Life expectancy, infant mortality, literacy and access to water are **social indicators**, because they tell you about people's health and education rather than about money directly.
## One number is never enough

Each indicator on its own can be misleading. GDP per capita is an **average**, so it hides inequality. If a few people in a country are extremely rich and most people are very poor, the average can look healthy even though most people are struggling. GDP also only counts things that are bought and sold, so it misses the work of a farmer growing food for her own family. Life expectancy can be dragged down by a single event, such as a war or an epidemic, even if other things are improving.

To get a fuller picture, the United Nations created the **Human Development Index (HDI)** in 1990. It combines three things into a single score between 0 and 1: **health** (life expectancy), **education** (years of schooling) and **income** (wealth per person). The closer the score is to 1, the more developed the country. The highest-scoring countries, such as Iceland, Norway and Switzerland, score above 0.95. The UK scores about 0.94. The lowest-scoring countries, such as South Sudan, Somalia and Niger, score around 0.4.
## Labels and lines

You will hear different words for groups of countries. 'Developed' and 'developing' are common, but many geographers prefer groups based on income. **HICs** are high-income countries, such as the UK, Japan and Canada. **LICs** are low-income countries, such as Niger, Chad and Malawi. In between are countries whose economies are growing quickly, sometimes called **NEEs** (newly emerging economies), such as China, India, Brazil and Nigeria.

In 1980 a report drew the **Brandt Line** across the world map, dividing a rich 'North' from a poorer 'South'. It is now out of date. The line had to loop round Australia and New Zealand, which are rich even though they are in the south, and since 1980 countries such as South Korea and Singapore have become very rich.

The word 'developing' can also give the wrong impression: that those countries are behind in everything. They are not. Kenya launched M-Pesa, a system for paying and sending money by mobile phone, in 2007 — years before paying by phone became normal in the UK.
## Why it matters

Comparing indicators helps governments and charities decide where help is most needed and check whether things are getting better. And many things are: across the world, the number of children who die before their fifth birthday has more than halved since 1990. Development is not fixed. Countries change — and indicators are how we measure it.

keywords.def: The progress a country makes in improving the lives of its people — wealth, health, education and freedom.
A statistic used to compare development between countries, e.g. life expectancy.
The value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by its population. An economic indicator.
The number of babies per 1,000 live births who die before their first birthday.
Human Development Index: combines life expectancy, education and income into a score from 0 to 1.
High-income country / newly emerging economy / low-income country.

questions.q: What is GDP per capita?
options: The number of people in a country
The value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by its population
The amount of money a country owes to other countries
The average wage of a factory worker
questions.explain: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a year. Dividing it by the population ('per capita' means 'per head') gives a rough measure of wealth per person.

questions.q: Which of these is a social indicator rather than an economic one?
options: GDP per capita
Value of exports
Literacy rate
Average income
questions.explain: Literacy rate tells you about education, so it is a social indicator. The other three are all about money, so they are economic indicators.

questions.q: Which three things does the Human Development Index (HDI) combine?
options: Health, education and income
Population, area and climate
Exports, imports and debt
Crime, housing and transport
questions.explain: HDI combines life expectancy (health), years of schooling (education) and income per person into one score between 0 and 1.

questions.q: What does the infant mortality rate measure?
options: The number of babies born each year
The average age at which women have children
The percentage of children who go to school
The number of babies per 1,000 live births who die before their first birthday
questions.explain: Infant mortality is a powerful indicator because it reflects healthcare, clean water, nutrition and education all at once.

questions.q: In Country X, a small number of people are extremely rich and most people are very poor. Why might its GDP per capita give a misleading picture?
options: It is an average, so it hides how unequally the wealth is shared
GDP per capita only counts poor people
GDP per capita is measured in the wrong currency
It only includes people living in cities
questions.explain: Because it is an average, a few very rich people can push the figure up, even if most people are struggling. That is why geographers never rely on one indicator.

questions.q: Country A has an HDI of 0.45 and Country B has an HDI of 0.92. Which statement is most likely to be true?
options: Country A is larger than Country B
Country A has a higher life expectancy
Country B probably has higher life expectancy and more years of schooling
Country B must have a hotter climate
questions.explain: The closer HDI is to 1, the more developed the country. Because HDI includes health and education, a score of 0.92 suggests longer lives and more schooling than 0.45. It says nothing about size or climate.

questions.q: Why is HDI usually a better measure of development than GDP per capita on its own?
options: It is easier to calculate
It includes health and education as well as wealth, giving a fuller picture
It only uses data from rich countries
It never changes from year to year
questions.explain: Development is about more than money. By combining health, education and income, HDI gives a more rounded picture than a single economic figure.

questions.q: Why is the Brandt Line now seen as out of date?
options: It was drawn in the wrong ocean
All countries are now equally rich
It only included European countries
Some countries in the 'South', like South Korea and Singapore, have since become rich
questions.explain: The world has changed since 1980. Several countries placed in the poorer 'South' have developed rapidly, so a simple North/South line no longer fits.

questions.q: GDP per capita is around $49,000 in the UK and around $600 in Niger. Roughly how many times larger is the UK's figure?
options: About 8 times
About 49 times
About 800 times
About 80 times
questions.explain: 49,000 ÷ 600 ≈ 82, so about 80 times larger. A quick way: 600 × 80 = 48,000, which is close to 49,000.

questions.q: In Country Y, 30 out of every 1,000 babies die before their first birthday. In the UK, it is about 4. Which statement is correct?
options: Country Y's rate is about twice the UK's
Country Y's rate is between 7 and 8 times the UK's
Country Y's rate is about 26 times the UK's
Country Y's rate is about 120 times the UK's
questions.explain: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5, so between 7 and 8 times higher. (30 − 4 = 26 is the difference, not how many times bigger — a common mix-up.)

sessions.reflect: Choose two development indicators. For each one, write a sentence explaining what it tells you about life in a country — and one thing it doesn't tell you.

read.title: Reading the periodic table like a map
read.intro: Rows, columns and a staircase line: how one chart lets you predict how an element will behave.
body: You already know that the periodic table lists every element in order of atomic number — the number of protons in its atoms. But the table isn't just a list. Its shape has been designed so that its position tells you about an element, in the same way that a grid reference on a map tells you about a place. To use it, you need to know three things: what the columns mean, what the rows mean, and where the metals end and the non-metals begin.
## Columns are groups

The vertical columns are called **groups**. The most important ones at this stage are numbered from **Group 1** on the far left to **Group 7**, with **Group 0** on the far right. (Some tables number them differently, calling the last group 8 or 18, but they mean the same thing.) In the middle is a wide block of metals called the **transition metals**, which includes many familiar ones: iron, copper, nickel, silver and gold.

Here is the key idea: **elements in the same group have similar chemical properties**. Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in Group 1. All three are soft metals that you can cut with a knife, and all three react with water, fizzing and giving off hydrogen gas. Helium, neon and argon are in Group 0. All three are colourless gases that hardly react with anything at all. If you know how one member of a group behaves, you can make a good prediction about the others.

Why does this happen? It is all to do with electrons. Electrons are arranged around the nucleus in layers called **shells**, and when atoms react, it is the electrons in the outermost shell that take part. Elements in the same group have the **same number of electrons in their outer shell**. For Groups 1 to 7, the group number tells you how many: every Group 1 element has 1 outer electron, and every Group 7 element has 7. Group 0 elements have a full outer shell, which is why they are so unreactive.
## Rows are periods

The horizontal rows are called **periods**. Period 1 contains just two elements, hydrogen and helium. Period 2 runs from lithium to neon, and period 3 from sodium to argon. As you move from left to right along a period, the atomic number goes up by one each time.

The period number tells you how many electron shells an atom has. Sodium is in period 3, so its atoms have 3 shells. Because sodium is in Group 1, it has just 1 electron in its outer shell. Its position — period 3, Group 1 — tells you both facts at once.
## The staircase line: metals and non-metals

Most periodic tables have a zig-zag 'staircase' line running down the right-hand side, starting near boron. **Metals** are found to the left of the line and in the middle of the table. **Non-metals** are found to the right of it. More than three-quarters of all elements are metals. The odd one out is hydrogen: it usually sits at the top left, but it is a non-metal gas.

Metals and non-metals have very different properties. **Metals** are usually shiny when freshly cut or polished. They are good **conductors** of heat and electricity, which is why saucepans and electrical wires are made of metal. They are **malleable**, meaning they can be hammered into shape without breaking, and **ductile**, meaning they can be stretched into wires. Most have high melting points, so they are solid at room temperature, and many are **sonorous** — they ring when you hit them, like a bell.

**Non-metals** are usually the opposite. They tend to be dull rather than shiny. Most are poor conductors of heat and electricity, so they are good **insulators**. When solid, they are usually **brittle**: a lump of yellow sulfur crumbles if you hit it with a hammer. Most have low melting and boiling points — eleven non-metals, including oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine, are gases at room temperature.

Metals and non-metals also form different kinds of oxides. When metals burn, they usually form oxides that are **bases**, which can neutralise acids. When non-metals burn, they usually form oxides that are **acidic**. Carbon dioxide, for instance, dissolves in water to make a weak acid.
## Exceptions to watch out for

Chemistry has rules, but it also has exceptions — and examiners love asking about them. **Mercury** is a metal, but it is a liquid at room temperature; it was once used in thermometers. **Bromine** is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature. **Graphite**, a form of carbon, is a non-metal that conducts electricity, which is why it is used in some batteries. And elements right next to the staircase line, such as silicon, have properties partly in between; they are sometimes called **metalloids**. Silicon is used to make computer chips.
## Using the table

Suppose you are told about a mystery element in period 3, Group 2. Find period 3 (it starts with sodium), move to the Group 2 column, and you land on **magnesium**. Without ever seeing it, you can now predict that it is a metal, that it conducts electricity, and that it reacts in a similar way to calcium, which is also in Group 2. That is the real power of the periodic table: it turns 118 separate facts into one pattern you can use.

keywords.def: A vertical column. Elements in the same group have similar properties and the same number of outer electrons.
A horizontal row. The period number tells you how many electron shells an atom has.
The block of metals in the middle of the table, e.g. iron, copper and gold.
A material that lets heat or electricity pass through it easily. Most metals are good conductors.
Can be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking.
Breaks or shatters easily when hit. Typical of solid non-metals.

questions.q: What are the vertical columns in the periodic table called?
options: Periods
Shells
Groups
Blocks
questions.explain: Columns are groups; rows are periods. A handy way to remember: a period comes at the end of a line of writing, which runs across.

questions.q: Where are the metals found in the periodic table?
options: On the left and in the middle
Only in the top row
On the right-hand side
Only in Group 0
questions.explain: Metals are to the left of the staircase line and in the middle (the transition metals). Non-metals are to the right. More than three-quarters of elements are metals.

questions.q: Which property is typical of non-metals?
options: Shiny
Malleable
Good conductor of electricity
Poor conductor of electricity
questions.explain: Most non-metals are poor conductors (insulators). Shiny, malleable and good conductor are all typical properties of metals.

questions.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
options: Mercury
Iron
Sodium
Bromine
questions.explain: Mercury is the metal that is liquid at room temperature. Bromine is also a liquid — but it is a non-metal, so it doesn't fit the question.

questions.q: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water in a similar way. Why?
options: They are all in the same period
They are all gases
They are all in the same group, so they have the same number of outer electrons
They all have the same number of protons
questions.explain: They are all in Group 1, so each has 1 electron in its outer shell. The outer electrons decide how an element reacts. (Each element has a different number of protons.)

questions.q: Element X is a dull yellow solid. It crumbles when hit and does not conduct electricity. What is it most likely to be?
options: A transition metal
A non-metal
A Group 1 metal
A metal alloy
questions.explain: Dull, brittle and non-conducting are all non-metal properties. This describes sulfur.

questions.q: Graphite conducts electricity. Why is this surprising?
options: Graphite is a form of carbon, a non-metal, and most non-metals don't conduct
Graphite is a metal, and metals don't conduct
Graphite is a liquid
Graphite is in Group 0
questions.explain: Carbon is a non-metal, and most non-metals are insulators, so graphite is an exception. Exceptions like this, mercury and bromine are popular exam questions.

questions.q: An element is in period 3 and Group 2. Which element is it?
options: Beryllium
Calcium
Aluminium
Magnesium
questions.explain: Period 3 starts with sodium (Group 1); next along is magnesium (Group 2). Beryllium is in Group 2 but period 2, calcium is in Group 2 but period 4, and aluminium is in period 3 but Group 3.

questions.q: Four elements have these melting points: A −7 °C, B 1,085 °C, C −218 °C, D 115 °C. Which is most likely to be a metal?
options: A
B
C
D
questions.explain: Most metals have high melting points, so B (1,085 °C — this is copper) is the best answer. A is bromine, C is oxygen and D is sulfur — all non-metals with low melting points.

questions.q: A sodium atom has 3 electron shells, with 1 electron in its outer shell. Where is sodium in the periodic table?
options: Group 3, period 1
Group 1, period 1
Group 1, period 3
Group 3, period 3
questions.explain: The number of shells gives the period (3), and the number of outer electrons gives the group (1). So sodium is in Group 1, period 3.

sessions.reflect: Pick an element you use every day — in a saucepan, a wire, a balloon or a pencil. Explain how its properties make it useful, using the word 'metal' or 'non-metal'.

sessions.subject: History

read.title: Stolen lives: the transatlantic slave trade
read.intro: This is a difficult topic. It matters because it shaped the modern world — including Britain.
body: Between the early 1500s and the 1860s, an estimated 12.5 million African men, women and children were forced onto ships and carried across the Atlantic Ocean to be enslaved in the Americas. It was the largest forced movement of people by sea in history. Britain was not a bystander. For much of the 1700s, British ships carried more enslaved Africans than those of any other country — over 3 million people in total.
## A new kind of slavery

Slavery had existed in many societies long before this, including ancient Greece and Rome. What made the transatlantic system different was its enormous scale and the fact that it was based on race. Enslaved Africans were treated as **chattel** — property that could be bought, sold and inherited, like furniture or cattle. They were enslaved for life, and their children were born into slavery too. To justify this, Europeans developed racist ideas claiming that Africans were less than fully human. Those ideas outlived slavery itself.
## The triangular trade
The trade is often described as a **triangle**, because ships made a three-part journey.

On the **first leg**, ships left British ports such as London, Bristol and Liverpool, loaded with manufactured goods: cloth, guns, iron and copper goods, and alcohol. On the west coast of Africa, these goods were exchanged for captured people. Some African rulers and merchants took part, selling prisoners taken in wars and raids, but it was European demand that drove the trade to such a vast scale. Captives were often held in forts along the coast, such as Cape Coast Castle in present-day Ghana, before being forced onto ships.

The **second leg** was the voyage across the Atlantic to the Caribbean and the Americas, known as the **Middle Passage**. It usually took six to eight weeks, sometimes much longer. Captives were chained together below deck, packed so tightly that they could barely move, with little air, food or water. Disease spread quickly. Of the roughly 12.5 million people forced onto ships, around 10.7 million survived the crossing.

On arrival, survivors were sold at auction, often separating families for ever. Most were taken to **plantations** — huge farms growing sugar, tobacco, cotton or coffee. Enslaved people worked long hours in exhausting heat under the constant threat of violent punishment.

On the **third leg**, ships returned to Britain carrying goods produced by enslaved labour, above all sugar, as well as tobacco, cotton and rum. Sugar went from being a luxury to something ordinary British families put in their tea every day. The profits helped Liverpool and Bristol grow rich, paid for grand country houses, and helped fund banks and businesses that still exist today.
## Resistance

Enslaved Africans resisted from the very beginning. Some rose up against ship crews during the Middle Passage. On plantations, people ran away, worked slowly, broke tools, and kept their own music, languages and beliefs alive despite every attempt to erase them. In Jamaica, communities of escaped people, known as **Maroons**, fought the British army for decades to stay free.

The most successful uprising was the **Haitian Revolution** (1791–1804). In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, enslaved people led by **Toussaint Louverture** rose up, defeated the armies sent against them, and in 1804 founded **Haiti**, the first independent nation created by formerly enslaved people. In Jamaica in 1831–32, **Samuel Sharpe** led a rebellion of tens of thousands of enslaved people. It was brutally crushed and Sharpe was executed, but it shocked the British government.
## Abolition

In Britain, a campaign to **abolish** the trade grew from the 1780s. Quakers were among the first to organise. **Thomas Clarkson** gathered evidence from sailors and doctors. Campaigners printed a diagram of the slave ship *Brookes*, showing how hundreds of people were packed into its hold; it shocked the public and was copied all over the country. **Olaudah Equiano**, who had been enslaved and later bought his freedom, published his life story in 1789; it became a bestseller and showed British readers the reality from an African point of view. **William Wilberforce**, a Member of Parliament, put forward bills to end the trade year after year. Ordinary people signed petitions, and hundreds of thousands refused to buy sugar grown by enslaved people.

One case became especially notorious. In 1781, the crew of the slave ship *Zong* threw more than 130 enslaved Africans overboard. The ship's owners then went to court to claim insurance money for them, as if they were lost cargo.

In **1807**, Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act, making it illegal for British ships to carry enslaved people. But slavery itself continued in British colonies. It was only with the **Slavery Abolition Act of 1833** that slavery was abolished across most of the British Empire, and even then most formerly enslaved people were forced to keep working unpaid as 'apprentices' until 1838. The government paid £20 million in compensation — not to the people who had been enslaved, but to the slave owners, for the loss of their 'property'. The loan Britain took out to pay it was so large that it was only finally paid off in 2015.
## Why we study it

The transatlantic slave trade explains a great deal about the world today: where people live, why some places are rich and others poor, and where racist ideas came from. It is also a story of extraordinary courage — of people who resisted, survived and fought for freedom against overwhelming odds.

keywords.def: A system where enslaved people are owned as property for life, and their children are born enslaved.
The three-part voyage: Britain to West Africa, Africa to the Americas, and the Americas back to Britain.
The voyage carrying enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas.
A large farm growing a single crop such as sugar or cotton, worked by enslaved people.
Officially ending something. Abolitionists campaigned to end the slave trade and slavery.
The uprising (1791–1804) in which enslaved people overthrew slavery and founded Haiti.

questions.q: Roughly how many Africans were forced onto ships during the transatlantic slave trade?
options: About 1 million
About 3,000
About 12.5 million
About 50 million
questions.explain: Historians estimate around 12.5 million people were forced onto ships between the 1500s and the 1860s. British ships carried over 3 million of them.

questions.q: What was the Middle Passage?
options: The voyage carrying enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to the Americas
The journey from Britain to West Africa
A road across the Sahara Desert
The route ships took back to Britain
questions.explain: It was the 'middle' leg of the triangular trade, and the most deadly: around 1.8 million people died on the crossing.

questions.q: What did ships mainly carry on the final leg, back to Britain?
options: Guns, cloth and alcohol
Gold and ivory
Tea and spices from India
Sugar, tobacco and cotton
questions.explain: The return leg carried goods produced by enslaved labour on plantations. Guns, cloth and alcohol were taken out to Africa on the first leg.

questions.q: What is meant by 'chattel slavery'?
options: Slavery that only lasted for a few years
People were owned as property for life, and their children were born enslaved
Working for low wages in a factory
Being forced to serve in the army
questions.explain: 'Chattel' means property. Under chattel slavery, people could be bought, sold and inherited, and slavery passed from parents to children.

questions.q: What did the 1807 Slave Trade Act do?
options: It freed all enslaved people in the British Empire
It paid compensation to enslaved people
It made it illegal for British ships to carry enslaved people, but slavery itself continued
It ended slavery in the USA
questions.explain: 1807 ended Britain's trade in enslaved people, but people already enslaved in British colonies stayed enslaved until the 1833 Act — and even then, compensation went to the owners, not the enslaved.

questions.q: Why did abolitionists print the diagram of the slave ship Brookes?
options: To advertise voyages to the Caribbean
To show the public how cruelly people were packed on board and build support for abolition
To help design bigger ships
To teach sailors how to load cargo
questions.explain: The image made the horror of the Middle Passage impossible to ignore. It was one of the first examples of a campaign using a powerful picture to change public opinion.

questions.q: Why was the Haitian Revolution so significant?
options: Enslaved people overthrew slavery and founded an independent nation
It ended the slave trade in Britain
It was a war between Britain and France over sugar
It was led by William Wilberforce
questions.explain: Led by Toussaint Louverture, enslaved people defeated colonial armies and created Haiti in 1804 — proof that enslaved people could win their own freedom.

questions.q: The owners of the Zong tried to claim insurance money for the people their crew had killed. What does this show?
options: That insurance was cheap in the 1780s
That the ship had been badly built
That the people were passengers who had paid for tickets
That the law treated enslaved people as cargo, not as human beings
questions.explain: Claiming insurance as if for lost goods showed how slavery turned people into property in the eyes of the law. The case outraged campaigners and helped build the abolition movement.

questions.q: How many years passed between the Slave Trade Act (1807) and the Slavery Abolition Act (1833)?
options: 16 years
36 years
31 years
26 years
questions.explain: 1833 − 1807 = 26 years. For those 26 years, the trade was illegal but people already enslaved in British colonies stayed enslaved.

questions.q: About 12.5 million people were forced onto ships and about 10.7 million survived the voyage. Roughly how many people died during the Middle Passage?
options: About 1.8 million
About 0.8 million
About 2.3 million
About 10.7 million
questions.explain: 12.5 − 10.7 = 1.8 million people — around one in every seven who were forced onto the ships.

sessions.reflect: Many different people helped to end the slave trade: enslaved people who resisted, formerly enslaved writers like Olaudah Equiano, and campaigners in Britain. Which do you think mattered most, and why?

sessions.subject: Geography
sessions.topic: Why are some countries poorer than others?

read.title: The development gap: why are some countries poorer?
read.intro: There is never just one reason. Physical and human factors usually work together.
body: In 1960, South Korea was roughly as poor as Ghana. Today South Korea is home to global companies like Samsung and Hyundai, and its people are among the wealthiest in Asia. Ghana has grown too, but much more slowly. Why do some countries race ahead while others fall behind? The difference in development between the richest and poorest countries is called the **development gap**, and explaining it is one of the big questions in geography.

There is no single cause. Usually several factors work together, and geographers sort them into two kinds: **physical factors**, to do with the natural environment, and **human factors**, to do with people, history and decisions.
## Physical factors

**Being landlocked.** A landlocked country has no coastline. To sell its goods abroad, it has to transport them across at least one other country to reach a port, which adds cost, paperwork and delay — and depends on staying on good terms with its neighbours. Africa has 16 landlocked countries, including Chad, Niger and Malawi, and many of them are among the poorest in the world.

**Climate and natural hazards.** In the Sahel, the dry region just south of the Sahara Desert, droughts can destroy crops and kill livestock, leaving families without food or income. Other countries face tropical storms, floods or earthquakes. A rich country can usually rebuild quickly after a disaster, but a poor one can lose years of progress. When a powerful earthquake struck Haiti in 2010, well over 100,000 people died and much of the capital was destroyed; the country is still recovering.

**Disease.** Some diseases thrive in hot, wet climates. **Malaria**, spread by mosquitoes, kills over half a million people every year, most of them young children in Africa. When people are often ill, adults cannot work and children miss school, which keeps families poor.
## Human factors

**Colonialism.** By 1914, European countries controlled almost all of Africa; only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent. Colonies were run for the benefit of the colonising countries, not the people who lived there. Railways were built to carry raw materials from mines and plantations to the coast for export, rather than to link towns together. European leaders drew many of Africa's borders at the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, often in straight lines across the map, splitting some peoples apart and pushing rival groups together — which contributed to conflicts later. When most colonies became independent in the 1950s and 1960s, many had economies that depended on exporting just one or two raw materials.

**Trade.** Many poorer countries still earn most of their money by exporting **primary products** — raw materials such as cocoa, coffee, cotton or copper. The trouble is that most of the money is made later, when raw materials are processed into finished goods. Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire grow around 60% of the world's cocoa, yet most of the money from a chocolate bar goes to the companies that make, transport and sell it, usually in richer countries. Cocoa farmers often receive only a few pence from every pound spent. The prices of primary products also rise and fall sharply, so a country that depends on one crop can see its income collapse in a single bad year.

**Debt.** In the 1970s and 1980s, many poorer countries borrowed large amounts of money from banks and richer countries. When interest rates rose, the repayments became huge. Money that could have been spent on schools, hospitals and roads went on paying back loans instead. In 2005, rich countries agreed to cancel many of the debts owed by the world's poorest countries, but debt is still a problem for many of them today.

**Conflict and government.** War destroys roads, schools and hospitals, forces people to flee their homes, and scares away businesses that might have invested. Corruption, where people in power steal or misuse public money, means that money meant for services never reaches the people who need it. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) is a striking example. It has enormous mineral wealth, and produces around 70% of the world's cobalt, which is used in phone and electric-car batteries. Yet it is one of the poorest countries in the world, because decades of conflict and corruption mean little of that wealth reaches ordinary people.
## The cycle of poverty

These factors often feed into each other in a **cycle of poverty**. When most people earn very little, the government collects little tax. With little tax money, it cannot pay for good schools and hospitals. Without good schools and healthcare, people are more likely to be ill and less likely to gain skills, so they stay on low incomes — and the cycle begins again.

Breaking the cycle is hard, but not impossible. South Korea invested heavily in education, and moved from exporting raw materials to making manufactured goods such as ships, cars and electronics, which earn far more. Next week we will look at the different ways countries, charities and ordinary shoppers try to close the development gap.

keywords.def: The difference in development between the richest and the poorest countries.
Having no coastline. Goods must cross other countries to reach a port.
When a powerful country takes control of another country and rules it for its own benefit.
A raw material taken from the land or sea, e.g. cocoa, coffee, copper or fish.
When people in power use their position dishonestly, e.g. stealing public money.
When the effects of poverty (e.g. poor schools and health) make it harder to escape poverty.

questions.q: What is the development gap?
options: The distance between the equator and the poles
The difference in development between the richest and poorest countries
The time it takes a country to recover from a disaster
The gap between a country's imports and exports
questions.explain: The development gap is the difference in wealth, health and education between the most and least developed countries.

questions.q: Why is being landlocked a disadvantage for trade?
options: Landlocked countries cannot grow any crops
Landlocked countries are always too hot
Goods must cross other countries to reach a port, adding cost and delay
Landlocked countries are not allowed to trade
questions.explain: Without a coastline, exports have to travel through a neighbouring country to a port. That adds transport costs and paperwork, and the country depends on its neighbours staying friendly.

questions.q: What is a primary product?
options: A raw material such as cocoa, coffee or copper
A product made in a factory
The most important product a country sells
A service such as banking or tourism
questions.explain: Primary products are raw materials taken from the land or sea. They usually earn far less than the finished goods made from them.

questions.q: Which disease, spread by mosquitoes, kills over half a million people every year?
options: Cholera
Measles
Flu
Malaria
questions.explain: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes in hot, wet climates. Cholera is spread by dirty water, and measles and flu are passed from person to person.

questions.q: Which of these is a human factor, not a physical factor, in a country's development?
options: Frequent droughts
Debts from past loans
Being landlocked
Tropical storms
questions.explain: Debt comes from human decisions about borrowing and lending, so it is a human factor. Droughts, storms and location are physical (natural) factors.

questions.q: Ghana grows huge amounts of cocoa. Why does it earn relatively little from it?
options: Nobody wants to buy cocoa
Cocoa can only be sold inside Ghana
Ghana gives its cocoa away
Most of the value is added when the beans are made into chocolate, usually in other countries
questions.explain: Processing (turning beans into chocolate, packaging, marketing) is where most of the money is made, and it mostly happens in richer countries. Farmers get only a few pence per pound spent.

questions.q: How did colonialism shape transport in many African countries?
options: Railways were built to carry raw materials to the coast, not to link towns
Motorways were built between every city
No transport was built at all
Airports were built in every village
questions.explain: Colonial railways were built to export raw materials to Europe. That left many countries with transport that didn't connect their own towns and cities well.

questions.q: DR Congo has huge mineral wealth but is one of the poorest countries in the world. Which best explains this?
options: It has no minerals that anyone wants
It is too cold to mine
Conflict and corruption mean little of the wealth reaches ordinary people
It has a very small population
questions.explain: Natural resources alone don't make a country rich. If conflict and corruption stop the money being spent on people, the wealth flows elsewhere.

questions.q: In the cycle of poverty, what is most likely to happen when a government collects very little tax?
options: It has more money for schools and hospitals
It has less money for schools and hospitals
People earn higher wages
The country becomes landlocked
questions.explain: Less tax means less money for public services. Poorer schools and healthcare then keep incomes low, so the cycle continues.

questions.q: If a cocoa farmer receives 6p from a £1 chocolate bar, what percentage of the price is that?
questions.explain: £1 = 100p, so 6p out of 100p is 6%. The other 94p goes to the companies that process, transport, package and sell the chocolate — and to taxes.

sessions.reflect: Of all the causes of poverty in this article, which do you think is the hardest to fix? Explain why in two or three sentences.

sessions.subject: English

read.title: Animal Farm: more than a story about animals
read.intro: Who stands for whom, and what was Orwell warning us about? (If you haven't finished the book, there are spoilers.)
body: On the surface, *Animal Farm* is a simple story. The animals on Manor Farm rebel against their drunken, careless farmer, chase him away and try to run the farm themselves, as equals. George Orwell even gave the book the subtitle 'A Fairy Story'. But almost every character and event in it stands for something in real history. A story in which characters and events represent real people, events or ideas is called an **allegory**. To understand *Animal Farm* properly, you need to know the history it is based on.
## The real story behind the farm

In the early 1900s, Russia was ruled by an emperor called the Tsar, **Nicholas II**. Most Russians were very poor peasants and factory workers, while a small group lived in great wealth. In 1917 a revolution overthrew the Tsar, and the **communists**, led by **Vladimir Lenin**, took power. They were inspired by the ideas of the German thinker **Karl Marx**, who had argued that workers should rise up and share the wealth they produced. The revolution promised equality and a better life for ordinary people. Russia became the centre of a new country, the Soviet Union.

After Lenin died in 1924, two men competed to replace him. **Leon Trotsky** was a brilliant speaker and planner. **Joseph Stalin** was less inspiring, but he was skilled at quietly building up power. Stalin won. Trotsky was forced out of the country, blamed for all kinds of problems, and later murdered. Stalin ruled through fear, using secret police, fake trials and forced-labour camps. He launched huge plans to modernise industry, while millions of people died in famines. His government used **propaganda** — information designed to persuade people, often by twisting the truth — to convince people that life was getting better and that Stalin was always right.

Orwell was a socialist, so he believed in equality. But he had seen for himself how communists backed by Stalin turned on other left-wing groups during the Spanish Civil War, and he believed Stalin had betrayed the ideals of the revolution. Many people in Britain admired the Soviet Union at the time, and Orwell wanted to show them what he saw as the truth. He wrote *Animal Farm* in 1943–44, during the Second World War, when Britain and the Soviet Union were allies against Hitler. Several publishers turned it down for that reason. It was finally published in August 1945, just after the war in Europe ended.
## Who's who on the farm

**Mr Jones**, the neglectful farmer, represents **Tsar Nicholas II**. **Old Major**, the wise old boar whose dream of a world without humans inspires the rebellion, represents **Karl Marx** and **Lenin** — the ideas and the leader behind the revolution.

**Napoleon**, the pig who quietly takes control, represents **Stalin**. He is not a good speaker, but he secretly raises a litter of puppies, which grow into fierce dogs that act as his private guard. The **dogs** represent Stalin's **secret police**. **Snowball**, the clever, energetic pig who plans the windmill, represents **Trotsky**. Napoleon's dogs chase him off the farm, and from then on he is blamed for everything that goes wrong.

**Squealer**, a persuasive pig who can make any bad news sound good, represents **propaganda**. Whenever the animals have doubts, he explains them away, twisting facts and statistics until the animals are unsure what they remember.

**Boxer**, the enormously strong cart-horse, represents the loyal **working class**. He believes in the revolution completely, and his answer to every problem is to work harder and trust that Napoleon is always right. His fate, when his strength finally fails, is one of the most heartbreaking moments in the book.

Other animals stand for other groups. **Moses**, the raven who tells stories of Sugarcandy Mountain, a paradise animals go to when they die, represents **religion**. The **sheep**, who bleat 'Four legs good, two legs bad' over and over, represent people who repeat slogans without thinking. **Benjamin**, the old donkey, sees clearly what is happening but never acts. The neighbouring farmers, **Mr Frederick** and **Mr Pilkington**, represent **Hitler's Germany** and **Britain and its allies**.
## How power corrupts

After the rebellion, the animals paint **Seven Commandments** on the barn wall, including 'All animals are equal'. As the pigs take more power, the commandments are quietly changed, usually at night, so that whatever the pigs are already doing is allowed. By the end, only one commandment remains, and it has been twisted into a famous sentence that contradicts itself: all animals are equal, but some are 'more equal than others'. In the final scene, the other animals look from the pigs to the humans and back again, and can no longer tell the difference.
## Why it still matters

*Animal Farm* is about Russia, but its warning is much wider. It shows how a revolution that begins with hope can be taken over by people who want power for themselves; how those in power can use language and propaganda to rewrite history; and how dangerous it is when ordinary people stop asking questions. The book's big **themes** — power and corruption, propaganda and language, education and ignorance, and betrayal — are what make it worth reading more than 80 years after it was written.

keywords.def: A story in which characters and events represent real people, events or ideas.
The 1917 revolution that overthrew the Tsar and brought the communists to power.
A political idea, based on Karl Marx's writing, that property and wealth should be shared by everyone.
Information, often biased or false, used to persuade people to support a leader or idea.
Writing that mocks people or ideas to criticise them. Animal Farm is a satire of Stalin's Soviet Union.
A big idea that runs through a text, e.g. power and corruption.

questions.q: What is an allegory?
options: A story that is completely true
A poem that rhymes
A story in which characters and events represent real people, events or ideas
A story told from an animal's point of view
questions.explain: In an allegory, the surface story stands for something else. Animal Farm is about animals on a farm, but it represents the Russian Revolution and Stalin's rule.

questions.q: Which real events is Animal Farm mainly based on?
options: The French Revolution
The English Civil War
The First World War
The Russian Revolution and the rise of Stalin
questions.explain: The rebellion against Mr Jones mirrors the 1917 Russian Revolution against the Tsar, and Napoleon's rise mirrors Stalin's.

questions.q: Which character represents Stalin?
options: Napoleon
Snowball
Old Major
Boxer
questions.explain: Napoleon quietly builds power, uses his dogs (the secret police) to get rid of rivals, and rules through fear — just like Stalin.

questions.q: What does Squealer represent?
options: The working class
Propaganda: the way leaders twist facts to control what people believe
Religion
The Tsar
questions.explain: Squealer explains away every problem and rewrites the past. Orwell uses him to show how propaganda keeps a government in power.

questions.q: Snowball is chased off the farm, then blamed for everything that goes wrong. Which real event does this mirror?
options: The death of Lenin
The Tsar being overthrown
Stalin forcing Trotsky out and blaming him for problems
Hitler invading Russia
questions.explain: Trotsky was driven out of the Soviet Union and became a scapegoat for Stalin's failures. Having an enemy to blame helps a leader avoid criticism.

questions.q: Boxer works harder and harder and always trusts Napoleon. What is Orwell suggesting through him?
options: Hard work always gets rewarded
Horses are the cleverest animals
The leaders should have worked harder
Loyal working people believed in the revolution but were exploited and betrayed by their leaders
questions.explain: Boxer gives everything to the revolution and is treated as disposable when he can no longer work. Orwell shows how Stalin's regime exploited the loyalty of ordinary workers.

questions.q: The pigs secretly change the commandments on the barn wall. What is Orwell showing?
options: Leaders who control information can rewrite the rules — and the past — to suit themselves
The animals were bad at painting
Rules should never be written down
The pigs wanted to make the farm fairer
questions.explain: Because most animals can't read well or remember clearly, the pigs can change the rules and claim they were always that way. This links to the themes of propaganda, power and education.

questions.q: Why did several publishers turn down Animal Farm in 1944?
options: They thought it was too long
Britain and the Soviet Union were allies in the Second World War
Orwell was unknown and had never been published
Books about animals were banned
questions.explain: During the war, the Soviet Union was fighting Hitler alongside Britain, so publishers worried about printing a book that attacked Stalin.

questions.q: The sheep bleat 'Four legs good, two legs bad' loudly whenever an animal tries to argue. What is Orwell criticising?
options: Animals who are too noisy
People who disagree with their leaders
Using simple slogans to stop people thinking and debating
Farmers who keep too many sheep
questions.explain: A slogan repeated over and over can drown out real discussion. Orwell shows how leaders use catchy phrases to stop people questioning them.

questions.q: Benjamin the donkey understands what is happening on the farm but does nothing. What message might Orwell want readers to take from this?
options: Staying silent when you can see wrongdoing allows it to continue
Donkeys are wiser than pigs
It is always best not to get involved
Older animals should be in charge
questions.explain: Benjamin could warn the others but chooses not to. Orwell suggests that people who see the truth and stay silent share some responsibility for what happens.

sessions.reflect: The final commandment says some animals are 'more equal than others'. Explain in your own words why this sentence doesn't make sense — and why Orwell meant it not to.
